review:
[h1]Vaultborn Frontier: A Fallout 4 Deep Dive[/h1]

[b]Graphics: 8.5/10[/b]
[i]Fallout 4’s visuals strike a solid balance between scale and detail. The sprawling Commonwealth is packed with ruined skyscrapers, overgrown suburbs, and radioactive wastelands that still manage to look alive. Although it doesn’t rival linear, narrative-driven shooters in shader complexity, creative use of mods can easily push its aesthetics past many modern titles—if you’re willing to dive into the modding scene.[/i]

[b]Story & Role-Playing: 8/10[/b]
[spoiler][i]You emerge from Vault 111 searching for your kidnapped child—an emotional hook that quickly gives way to a sprawling power struggle between Minutemen, Brotherhood of Steel, Railroad, and Institute. Dialogue is streamlined compared to older Fallout entries, but investing in graphical and dialogue mods can restore deeper conversation trees and revive full-fledged role-play choices.[/i][/spoiler]

[b]S.P.E.C.I.A.L. & Character Creation: 9/10[/b]
[i]Fallout 4 delivers the most robust character builder in the series. Your S.P.E.C.I.A.L. stats shape every perk unlock, and the extensive face-customization sliders let you craft a survivor that looks—and feels—unique. While it leans more “shooter RPG” than “hardcore RPG,” your build still determines stealth, charisma checks, and crafting prowess in meaningful ways.[/i]

[b]Factions & Freedom: 7.5/10[/b]
[i]The four major factions each offer their own narrative arcs and end-game outcomes, but you can’t fully betray or erase some companion storylines—limiting the true sandbox freedom veteran RPG fans crave. Still, choosing who controls the Commonwealth remains a satisfying strategic choice that defines the final ending cinematic.[/i]

[b]Atmosphere: 8/10[/b]
[i]The Commonwealth’s mood swings from eerily silent vaults to tense skirmishes in bombed-out city streets. Environmental storytelling—rusting Ferris wheels, half-collapsed overpasses—cements that “post-nuclear” feel, although it rarely reaches the haunting resonance of Fallout 3’s more claustrophobic locales.[/i]

[b]Soundtrack & Ambient: 9.5/10[/b]
[i]Fallout 4 nails the nostalgic Americana vibe. From the plaintive croon of “The End of the World” (Skeeter Davis) to the defiant rock of “Crawl Out Through the Fallout,” the licensed tunes and ambient soundscapes (wind howls, Geiger crackles) pull you deep into an atomic-age wasteland.[/i]

[b]Gameplay & Mechanics: 9/10[/b]
[i]Combat feels tighter than prior installments—real-time gunplay fused with V.A.T.S. targeting offers both immediacy and tactical flair. Power Armor returns as a functional, upgradable exosuit complete with jet-pack mods. The Automatron DLC even lets you field customized robot companions, turning firefights into mechanical showdowns.[/i]

[b]World & Exploration: 9/10[/b]
[i]Every open door and crater rumbles with hidden loot, side-quests, and Easter eggs. While the map isn’t enormous, its dense layering of locations—settlements, vaults, roadside camps—yields hundreds of hours of discovery. Meticulous scavenging and maker-style crafting keep exploration endlessly rewarding.[/i]

[b]Settlement & Simulation: 9.5/10[/b]
[i]Fallout 4’s settlement system transforms you into a post-apocalyptic civil engineer. Build fortified colonies, manage resource flows, and recruit settlers—bridging city-builder mechanics with an end-of-the-world RPG. Creating your own castle and defending it with turrets and guard posts is a surprisingly addictive sandbox within the wasteland.[/i]

[b]Mods & DLC: 9/10[/b]
[i]Thanks to an active modding community, you can elevate Fallout 4’s visuals, add questlines, and overhaul gameplay systems. Official expansions—Far Harbor’s eerie island mystery, Nuka-World’s twisted amusement park—expand the story in memorable ways.[/i]

[b]Bugs & Stability: 7.5/10[/b]
[i]Bethesda’s engine still shows its wrinkles: quest scripts occasionally break, and heavy mod loads can trigger crashes. Yet careful load-order management and community patches smooth out most rough edges.[/i]

[b]Value & Replayability: 9.5/10[/b]
[i]With base game, DLC, and thousands of mods at your disposal, Fallout 4 delivers countless hours of role-play, base-building, and exploration—for a fraction of the cost of buying separate titles. Its open-ended design guarantees you’ll keep discovering new ways to play.[/i]

[h1]Overview[/h1]
[i]Fallout 4 blends shooter-style combat, deep RPG progression, and city-builder settlement management into a singular post-nuclear sandbox. While it sacrifices some narrative depth compared to its predecessors, its boundless crafting, robust mod scene, and evocative soundtrack make it a must-own for any wasteland wanderer.[/i]

[b]Total Score: 9.1★[/b]
[i]An essential open-world experience that pairs nostalgia with innovation—Fallout 4 remains a defining chapter in Bethesda’s RPG saga.[/i]

review:
When I first stepped into the world of Fallout 4, I did not step lightly.
The earth had been scorched, the skies forever dimmed, and the echoes of the old world still clung to the bones of broken cities. I had just lost all that was dear: [spoiler]my home, my love, and the child I swore to protect. In a single breath, the warmth of the past was turned to cold memory.[/spoiler]

And yet… I emerged. From the metal womb of Vault 111, into a world reborn in ruin.
The surface was not what it once was — no, it was something else entirely.
Alive. Chaotic. Honest.

Every step forward was a test. Sometimes, I survived with only my fists and will. Sometimes with a pipe pistol held together by rust and desperation. Other times, it was not my strength, but my words — a calm voice, a raised brow, a subtle gesture
that allowed me to walk away from a boiling conflict unscathed. In this world, a sharp tongue is often deadlier than a sharp blade.

The people? Oh, they are many and varied.
Some cling to ideals like rust clings to steel: zealots who pray to atomic gods, raiders who laugh at the sun,
scientists who twist the fabric of life in laboratories forgotten by time. And yet, some are simply lost: scavengers, builders, wanderers… like me. All seeking purpose in the post-apocalyptic dust.

[h1] Fallout 4 does not offer a paradise. It offers potential. [/h1]

You may choose to be a savior, a tyrant, a diplomat, or merely a tired soul gathering scrap to build a single, sturdy wall in a world where nothing stands for long. You can rebuild towns. You can ignite wars. You can even dress your dog in goggles and call it destiny.

Yes, it is a dark world. Yes, it reminds us painfully of what happens when greed outpaces wisdom. But in that desolation, there is also room for laughter, for stories by the campfire, for sarcastic robots and teddy bears holding cigars. 
It is a world as absurd as it is tragic.

Perhaps that is the lesson hidden in all the rubble:
Even after the bombs fall, even when all is lost there is still something worth fighting for.
And sometimes, something worth smiling about.

I keep trying to finish Fallout 4. I really do. I love Skyrim, and this is basically the same thing right?

Well.. that's exactly the problem. There are some superficially interesting factions, a metric fuckton of radiant quests, and an open world to explore. Throw in some retrofuturism and some irradiated zombies, and that's basically all Fallout 4 is. 

About 10 hours into FO4 I made a terrible mistake. I bought Fallout New Vegas. Now, I won't pretend that NV is the best thing ever. It isn't. It crashes like 10x more. But it does have better character dialogue and roleplaying potential.

In Fallout 4, you get to pick between 4 dialogue options:
1. exposition
2. being polite
3. being neutral
4. the Red Dead provoke option

This is one of those games where all the pre-launch promo is about how the game has so much freedom and then you play it and the "endless opportunities" are being Very Evil, True Neutral, or The Most Good Person Ever. 

This is War Never Changes: The Boring One. Combat shooting is better now, Nick Valentine is cool. The railroad suck, the minutemen suck, the institute characters are introduced too late, and the BoS feels rushed.

review:
[h1]Life is Strange 2 – 100% Completion Review[/h1]
[i]All achievements earned, all collectibles found, all endings unlocked across all episodes[/i]

[b]Life is Strange 2 is about choices, but not in the usual way.[/b]
It is not about what path you take. It is about what you teach someone else to become. Completing it fully brings that focus into sharp relief.

You play as Sean Diaz, a teenager forced on the run with his younger brother Daniel after a traumatic event. What follows is a road trip across a fractured America, one that uses politics, poverty, and prejudice not as backdrop, but as core themes. It pulls no punches, and while not every moment lands cleanly, the intent is clear and often powerful.

[b]Your relationship with Daniel is the real mechanic.[/b]
Dialogue, actions, tone, and consistency all shape his growth. He watches you. Learns from you. Mimics you. A full completion run means experiencing every version of who Daniel can become, and each ending hits harder for it.

[b]Exploration and collectibles are light, but meaningful.[/b]
Drawing moments return, and optional items unlock subtle worldbuilding. Achievements often tie to quiet, missable scenes that reveal who these characters really are.

Not every episode is equally strong. Some pacing issues linger, and the episodic structure shows its seams. But the emotional core stays steady throughout.

ice raids in the united states are currently at an all time high and i strongly recommend, if you can, attending a protest. if you are unaware what is going on in the united states right now, i strongly recommend educating yourselves as there are plenty of resources online. if you simply don't care, i strongly recommend getting your head out of your ass. 

if you've played the game, you know why i have decided to write that as my opening. if you haven't played the game, i recommend you do so, as it is still, in the great 2025, unfortunately relevant and could hopefully open your eyes to the perspectives of immigrant-born american citizens/immigrants.

this game is extremely heartbreaking and is a rollercoaster of emotions. i need to know more about the people who wrote this game and how many tears were shed over during the development of it. i can't imagine writing the story and not getting super attached and emotional over it. sean and daniel are my sons now. 

this is actually the last life is strange game i had lined up to finish. yes, i even played true colors AND double exposure before this. i don't know why i left this game last, but it did not impact the experience and does not tie into the other life is strange games... kind of. there are a couple of references and a life is strange 1 character does show up at some point during the game, but not knowing them will not impact your experience. 

that being said, this is my favorite life is strange game of all time. being a poc immigrant living in the south, means that i have also, at some point, experienced the racism sean and daniel experience in this game. albeit, not to the same extents, but it does make this game extremely relatable. and painful to play at times. 

living in the south also means that i am friends with a lot of other immigrant pocs too, mostly hailing from south america like sean and daniel. thinking of my family, friends, the people i love going through what the diaz family goes through in this game is heartbreaking. anyone going through that is heartbreaking. so much of what is on the news right now is BOTH documented and non-documented immigrants getting forcefully removed from the so-called "land of the free" for days on end. families being torn apart. millions of people in detention. an insane amount of racial profiling. it's disgusting what is going on right now. what daniel and sean go through? people are going through that in real life too. a million times worse! remember that.

i hope that you, reading this review, decide to play this game. it doesn't have to be anytime soon. in fact, you could watch a gameplay of it on youtube too. i think that if you personally have never experienced... racism or are bigoted but open to change, you should play this game. i think if you like hard, hitting stories, you should play it. if you like life is strange, play it. it's gay at times (i know our fanbase). i think everybody should play it. yes, like the other life is strange games/choice-based story games, it's pretty linear... but it's a linear ride through a good story. learn from this game.

name: Life is Strange 2
review:
I absolutely loved every single part of Life is Strange 2. The entire story was incredibly compelling, especially watching how the two brothers, Sean and Daniel, survived and learned about rights and wrongs through their journey. I honestly don't think there's a better game out there that so powerfully builds on the trust and bond between brothers, even when they're facing immense challenges.

Without the rewind mechanic that was in the first game, I really had to sit and think about every choice I was going to make. Knowing that once a decision was made, there was no going back, added such an intense layer to the gameplay. It genuinely made those choices feel weighty and impactful, and because of that, this game definitely begs for more than one playthrough to see all the different outcomes.

The emotional impact from this game was immense; it kept me on the edge of my seat the entire time. By the end, I even found myself crying, which really speaks to how deeply invested I became in their story. Life is Strange 2 is a masterclass in emotional storytelling and character development.

review:
For me, the road trip nature of the story just doesn't do it for me. The story of Life is Strange 2 follows a road trip and that means every episode the game desperately tries to set you up to connect with new characters quickly and it gets overwhelming and exhausting fast. For me to just go into these episodes, spend time and effort to get with the new characters and they're just gone the next episode... just feels not satisfying? 

At times the game can also feel like it's trying to include way too many elements, even at the expense of a good storytelling. The game covers social stigmas, sexuality, religion, racism etc which is of course a good thing to bring awareness to. But as a player it lead me really confused when the game throws in a considerable amount of screen time ([spoiler]Racist people going up your face in episode 1 and 4[/spoiler]) and writes character motivation ([spoiler]Sean being scared of how a police officer would perceive him[/spoiler]) related to these social issues, but none of it really get built up to be strong enough for a good emotional payoff. While it is good that they attempt to bring these discussions up among their players, these sub-themes are often just left hanging around and not building up to anything.

I also wish there were more parts about Karen. She genuinely feels like an authentic character

name: Life is Strange 2
review:
Why does this game have so many positive reviews?  According to global achievements:
Only 40% of the people who purchase the game finish chapter 1
Only 20% of purchasers actually finish the game
I think likely <2% of the people who see this game for what it is and don't agree with its political message go on to finish the game and write up an honest review that gets seen by potential buyers.  I decided to be part of that 2% and give my truthful analysis of what this is.

I am one of the folks who was so moved by the first game that I immediately checked out the 2nd game, saw the good reviews, and went ahead to give it a try since it was on sale.

They abandoned the mechanics of the first game that gave you control of a super power which allowed you to rewind and explore different dialogue options and moral approaches to situations.  This is what fundamentally made the first game so interesting and addicting.

Instead, you get a glorified babysitting simulator where your little brother has control of the superpower (his dialogue and personality are insufferable to most players according to other reviews and myself) that is laced from beginning to end with identity politics propaganda, essentially a complete checklist of all the radical left talking points surrounding the 2016 election and following years.

The game is packed with racist stereotypes of conservative Americans.  The protagonist is beat up / harassed / humiliated by "racist rednecks" numerous times through the chapters and each chapter begins with a storyboard that tries to explain how Sean and his brother are being "hunted down" by the evil police and racists.  The further you go into the game, the cringier the identity politics political messaging gets.  By the end, it completely replaces any meaningful story about the characters.

Apart from chapter 2, the only "good" Caucasian characters are portrayed as those rejected by mainstream society [spoiler](your allies in chapter 3 are a gang of purple hair, face-tatted, nose ring equipped druggies living in a homeless camp - and chapter 5 a burning-man style desert commune that even goes as far as including a gay couple who claims it's incredibly dangerous to be gay in America - and lets not forget the neckbeard in chapter 1 who tells you EVERYTHING is about politics now)  They even go out of their way to bring back the only assertive male LiS 1 character David who they portray as a desert hippie who's rejected his evil ways. [/spoiler],

And outside of the constant political pandering, the pace of the story doesn't feel right, there's not really any consistent character development outside of the protagonist since they are on a road trip to escape the evil police and constantly on the move, and the dialogue is awkward and clunky.  The glitches and wonky looking facial expressions really kick in at chapter 5 and you can tell they gave up fixing it because so few people were finishing the game.

So there's two types of people having a go at this game : Type 1 : Since the summer of 2015, your brain has been melted by the onslaught of identity politics propaganda being funneled into your life and you're going to give this game a thumbs-up regardless of how far you got in it.  Type 2 : You stopped watching/believing the news after 2016 and you're still able to think for yourself, you immediately see this game for what it is, and 98% of you give up before the end of chapter 1.  Take a careful look at the positive reviews and see for yourself.  This game, and the vast majority of the positive reviews for it are all just essentially a scam trying to promote a piece of interactive political propaganda.

name: Life is Strange 2
review:
Where is home?

That’s the big question you’ll keep asking in Life is Strange 2. Sean and Daniel hit the road from Seattle to Puerto Lobos, trying to figure out what home really means. At one point, home was a safe, loving place with their dad—a simple but happy life.

As they travel, they go through all sorts of experiences. Sometimes they’re on their own, and other times they meet up with distant family. They even spend time off the grid with a group of hippies, and at one point, Daniel gets caught up in a cult. Throughout the game, they don’t really have a permanent home until the very end.

They make some tough choices and challenge the justice system, but in the end, they find a sense of belonging. In a world that feels pretty hostile, running away seems to be their only option.

LiS2 is definitely different from the original Life is Strange. Sean’s life is way tougher compared to Max’s more typical high school experience. That contrast makes both stories unique and enjoyable in their own ways.

I do wish LiS2 highlighted the consequences of choices a bit more. In the first game, decisions could seriously affect the life of a friend and even the town of Arcadia Bay, but here it feels less impactful.

Also, I wanted more closure in the endings. There aren’t any updates about characters like the grandparents or Brody years after the events at the border. I really wanted to know how those who helped the brothers were doing at the end.

But overall, I had a blast playing the game.

name: Life is Strange 2
review:
I know the second game has far fewer fans than the first, and I get why. It has a different pace, different characters. There’s less Twin Peaks and more real America. It gets a lot of criticism, but I want to praise it instead. Maybe even overlook some of its rough edges, because Life is Strange 2 is a unique experience I genuinely want to recommend to everyone.

The story doesn’t hold back. It starts in warmth, in the comfort of a loving family. But within minutes, everything falls apart. Safety becomes a memory, replaced by the road — long, dangerous, and filled with impossible choices. The emotional weight doesn’t build by episode — it builds by the second. At some point, you think: that’s it, this is rock bottom. And then the game hits harder.

This isn’t just a story about brothers, the road, or superpowers. It’s about humanity, about choices, and the cost of kindness. There are no perfect answers. There’s just you, your little brother, and a world that isn’t always willing to make space for you. And all you have is each other.

One of the game’s biggest strengths is its visual style. It’s rougher, less “cozy-vintage” than the first one. But that’s intentional. The scenery keeps shifting — forests, deserts, makeshift shelters, strangers’ homes. Everything’s constantly in motion, just like the characters. Sometimes it’s bleak, sometimes stunningly beautiful. In those landscapes, you can feel the loneliness, the running, but also life, raw and real.

The music? Pure love. Every song is carefully chosen and hits just right. You’ll want to play them on repeat. They wrap around the atmosphere perfectly, right when they need to.

The gameplay is quiet, unobtrusive — it lets you truly step into the role of an older brother who isn’t just surviving, but teaching someone else how to live. That’s the core of it: you’re not just choosing dialogue. You’re shaping a personality, a moral compass, a child’s response to a brutal world. And because of that, the consequences hit differently — they feel like your responsibility.

Life is Strange 2 isn’t a perfect game. It has its flaws — some episodes drag, some plot twists feel abrupt. But even so, it deserves love. If nothing else, because every ending leaves you with a lesson that matters.

name: Life is Strange 2
review:
It's hard to believe that anyone might not know what the first “Life is Strange” game was. It stands out as one of only 14 games, out of the 629 that I own, to which I have given a score above 9.5/10, and it is undoubtedly the best game in the Life is Strange franchise. The game is a third-person adventure where the player controls a character.

In "Life is Strange 2," the main character is a 17-year-old boy named Sean. The player interacts with the surrounding world, communicates with other NPCs, and performs actions that advance the game's storyline.
The plot is divided into episodes (here there are five plus a prologue), each set-in different environments and often featuring different NPCs. The only constant is the presence of Sean and his younger brother, Daniel, who is revealed in the prologue to have telekinesis powers. Although initially unknown, this power becomes increasingly significant as the game progresses.

The core of the game is not the power itself, but the interaction and relationship between the two brothers. The player’s choices and actions will influence their relationship throughout the game and determine the ending. Therefore, the choices are fundamental and should reflect how the player wants the main character to behave.

Unlike "Life is Strange 1," where the drama unfolds later in the game, players are immersed in a whirlwind of emotions from the prologue in "Life is Strange 2." While I don't want to compare this game to its predecessor too much, I consider both to be excellent games, even though I personally find "Life is Strange 1" superior to "Life is Strange 2".
I found Chloe (from LIS 1) to be more compelling than Sean, whom I felt was too submissive to his brother. Additionally, some parts of the storyline are hard to believe and overly filled with sad moments compared to LIS 1. Daniel is also challenging to manage, considering his young age of 9, and secondary characters often only appear for one episode, limiting the possibility of maintaining relationships with them.

If you loved “Life is Strange 1,” this second game is a must-buy, as it retains the same gameplay style. If you haven't played it before and are interested in these types of games, I recommend getting both.
As for the other titles in the Life is Strange series, I haven't played True Colors yet, so I can't comment on it, though it seems promising. However, I would advise against Double Exposure, which I have read is not worthy of the Life is Strange title.

The game takes about 12-20 hours to complete, depending on how much you enjoy reading, finding hidden objects for achievements, or talking to people. I believe a playtime of 15 hours is average.

Final rating: 8/10

review: I consider myself a fan of choice-based games, and among many of them, I feel a deep connection with Life is Strange 2. I believe this game resonates with my life due to the various situations and decisions one must face, and the consequences that come with them. I'm going to say something that risks my life but none the less I know it to be true... I prefer this to BG3.

I'm a sucker for 40K and that helps but the uniqueness of the universe adds a vastly different palette of colours to the playing experience that just isn't found anywhere else. You have to come at the game with vastly different expectations to what any other RPG requires and it brilliant for it.

I personally love the cast of characters for what they all bring to the story and adore the way it all weaves together to form what I felt was a great journey. 

Your choices matter and that, in this economy, is more valuable than gold. I felt the weight of my actions, the intended and unintended. It was so refreshing.

The combat was largely what I expected it to be but that's a win in my books, I love the almost X-Com-esk nature of it and really enjoyed trialing tactics and builds. 

I wont pretend there were no glitches, it's a big RPG with lots of moving parts, something is gonna break and it was never game breaking, 99% of them I quick-saved and loaded that save and it was fixed (hud issues mostly) but they were rare and not anything that made me upset but if you have no patience on these kinda things, be aware. 

All in all I loved the game 10/10, will be doing a drastically different run next and am excited to see how the game reacts this time around. 
You don't need to be a 40K fan but it helps that I am one.

name: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader
review:
Bloody hell. Oh yeah also this is a long review.

First off, to create the illusion of structure in this review I will begin with a seemingly unrelated statement: The worst game I've ever played in my entire life is Pathfinder: Kingmaker. That's right, leave your little clown emoji and jog on, losers. Okay, now it's just us, let's carry on.

I know of Warhammer 40k peripherally. I've never played any game in the universe before and have never played the tabletop miniatures stuff despite being nerdy enough to not only withstand but also win a 10 hour game of Twilight Imperium, and old enough to remember when the words "parallax scrolling" were cause for arousal. I bought Rogue Trader off the back of a work colleague's recommendation, at a point where I was waiting patiently for Date Everything to not get its release date delayed again, so I needed something to fill the void. 

I did not expect to be playing one of the best CRPGs I’ve ever seen in four decades of gaming.

You are a Rogue Trader, blah blah plot explanation. There is not one single facet of this game that is not at least very good in quality – the glory of Rogue Trader is/are the sheer amount of facets there are to enjoy. You have strong RPG elements, involving three core morality paths you can follow resulting in different outcomes, dialogue options stemming from your skills, background and companions. The companions are beautifully written – flawed and great and a mess all at the same time, and brilliantly voiced, with their own personal questlines to complete. And of course, the main story is bold, sprawling and epic, as befitting the setting.

But there is so much more to this game. First off, the combat. Have you ever wondered what it would be like if your soldiers in X-COM got to do like 15 actions every turn? Christ. I’m writing this review at the precise moment of me completing one run of the game, 140 hours. 97 of those hours are me ensuring that Kibellah never has less than 27 buffs on her every single combat, even the random warp ones where you’re up against three pink horrors. The vast majority of battles in Rogue Trader aren’t decided in the first few rounds – they’re decided in the first few turns. There is a character called Sister Argenta, and I cannot even describe to you what it is possible for her to do in a single turn, because it would be like when the walking miasma of nervous sweat and odour in the board game café starts explaining why he’s just beaten you at Yu-Gi-Oh. But here’s the important part: Argenta ain’t nothin without her queen, Cassia.

Warhammer 40k often comes across as such a violent, uncompromising universe of horror and heresy that, from the outside, it seems inconceivable that two people would even be able to sit down and have a cup of tea without pulling plasma pistols on each other within seconds and melting each others’ faces off. Yet Rogue Trader excels at showcasing the quieter, more nuanced aspects of 40k – the class divide, the endless politics, the intrigue and yes, the diplomacy. It also beautifully evokes the brotherhood and siege mentality that brings people together in even the most heinous and brutal circumstances. And this feeling of weathered, yet necessary companionship really translates into the combat – your allies are constantly buffing, supporting, protecting and directing each other, often more so than many other tactical squad games. For all her martial zeal, Argenta cannot navigate the battlefield alone (see what I did there?).

Better move on or I’ll hit the word limit. MUSIC – the music is insane. Prior to playing this game, if you could pluck from my brain the exact thread of consciousness responsible for conceiving of what the soundtrack to a 40k RPG should sound like, it would be identical to what has been put together in this project. The music is one of the most magnificent parts of this game – it is dark and brooding, it is holy and reverent, it is screaming with its guts all over the pentagram, it is telling you that you won’t survive unless you make damn sure nothing else does. An absolute triumph of noise that never lets up even in the quiet moments.

There are other gameplay elements that I was completely unaware of going into this game, too. There is ship combat that is fully fleshed out, with tactics and skills and environmental buffs. There is colony management, with hard decisions to be made when problems arise on them (pro tip it’s heresy it’s always heresy what else was it gonna be let’s be real). There is star system exploration with warp navigation management. There is trading with various factions to get the most powerful items in the game. There are secret companions. There is a lot of game to this game outside of the classic CRPG trappings, and it is ALL done really well. I didn't even talk about levelling up, one of the most bonkers parts! Oh well I'm tired.

And then just the little touches sprinkled everywhere, just small details too numerous to mention that make this an RPG that achieves the most important tenet of the genre - attention to detail. Despite my play time, my only (non) criticism of the game is that I wish there were more of everything. I wish you could have more dialogue options with your companions. I wish there were more star systems to explore. I wish there were DLC I could OH My GOD

So on top of all this, my jaw detached from my face and smashed on my keyboard halfway through my playthrough when I realised that Owlcat Games, the geniuses behind this project, are the same REPROBATES that made Pathfinder Kingmaker, not just the worst RPG ever made, but the worst GAME ever made! This is a better redemption arc than stupid No Man’s Sky, which is still a terrible game by the way, you’re all just giving A for effort like a doting pre-school teacher, get those reviews back on Not Recommended, now! Stand by some principles for god’s sake. What was I saying? Oh yeah this game rules – get it and purge some serious heresy. THE DIVINE WATCHES OOOOOOOOOVER UUUUUUUUUUS

name: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader
review:
I very much enjoyed the Rogue Trader CRPG and its expansions: Void Shadows and DLC. I came into the game as a Warhammer 40k neophyte, and while some of the importance of terms, people, and locations was lost on me during the first few playthroughs, I was compelled to stay by the twisting story and compelling characters. The ensemble cast of the Rogue Trader's retinue is a winning combination, because making interesting and varied characters is something that I think Owlcat does exceptionally well. Each new expansion has only added value to the game's replayability, so definitely don't skip Lex Imperialis or Void Shadows. 

My only gripe, and this is true of not just Rogue Trader and Owlcat's games in the Pathfinder series, but also any direct TTRPG ruleset to PC (including Baldur's Gate 1 and 2, Neverwinter Nights 1 and 2, Numenera, Shadowrun, and to a lesser extent BG3), is that I don't think the game's combat and player mechanics translate one to one as well as studios hope. My preference is for combat systems to be designed for the PC/console gaming experience, not a ruleset port with some optimization. But that shouldn't stop you from playing the game; after all, there's a LOT of story to get through, and you can find plenty of build guides to help you crush heretics.

name: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader
review:
Eh, I played a bit, but I think this is the end for Owlcat and me.

The look of their games, the characters, the writing, the plots: they're all aces, and I love that about a game, which is why they've gotten 3 tries with me so far, but I don't think they'll get a fourth.

Why?  Because their games are not RPGs, despite the settings and marketing.

Git gud!

OK, troglodyte, I think there's a misunderstanding here. See, I've played games from NES to now. I got the whole "develop muscle memory for one thing that translates to nothing else" out of the way with Battletoads. That's not why I'm playing games. It's why RPGs are one of my favorite genres of game.

While in theory these games are RPGs, in practice they are not. It's as though on the back end someone decided, "Well, we love this setting and have a great story, but you know what? 0.001% of min-maxing players will, because it's a video game, have an easy time of it.  So let's actively punish them for playing this in video game form by raising the difficulty 10 times higher than the pen and paper rules."  Pro-tip, that means all your players now have to min-max. Your idea of role-playing and picking just the kind of character you personally want to play went out the window when in order to progress past mid-game you need to research what companion skills will be on the table and types of weapons are going to become available and actually allow progress, and then create your character based on that.  It's not role-playing anymore.

And I appreciate that the same people doing the amazing writing aren't the ones making that decision, I don't want to imply that I think the studio itself is full of morons. That's clearly not the case, but there's obviously a disconnect between the "let's try and create platonic anti-fun" crowd at Owlcat, and the "we're creating a fun RPG that if you like these settings you're gonna love our game!" crowd. The problem is that in practice, the former group wins, but then when they're selling it they're pretending it's all the latter.

And hey, if that's your idea of a good time - if you're a min-maxer yourself and you like to see that rewarded, then good for you, you're gonna love these games if you like a game that rewards that wrapped up in fantastic writing. If you actually wanted a role-playing game, though, you're gonna be disappointed. A lot.

So all in all, not recommended. It is not what it says on the package.

Also, FYI, while the in-game documentation is copious and it should actually give you some idea of what everything is, the writing and organization of it is awful and it clarifies almost nothing. Maybe that's part of the licensing, though.  "Write in-game documentation SO BAD people will have to buy the rulebooks to actually understand things, and we'll let you use our name." It makes more sense as an explanation than anything else, honestly.

name: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader
review:
Coming from someone who had 0 exposure to Warhammer 40k lore before this, I’ll be straight, I only bought the game because I loved Owlcat's WoTR and damn, they didn’t disappoint. The game’s genuinely excellent, and credit where it’s due, Owlcat managed to drag me headfirst into the grimdark chaos of the 40k universe purely through their storytelling and quest design.

The writing? Top-tier. The quests? Complex and rewarding. Even as someone totally new to the setting, I never felt lost or confused.

That said, having finished WoTR twice before this, I can see the Owlcat signature all over the gameplay and puzzle design. The structure, the style of exploration, even in certain quest patterns, you can absolutely tell it’s the same team behind both games. But honestly? That just makes me even happier. It’s familiar without feeling like a copy-paste job, and it scratches that same itch WoTR did, but with enough new elements to stay exciting.

I also gotta say that the atmosphere and setting blew me away. Even with no 40K knowledge, the oppressive, brutal vibe, the insane characters, and the sheer weight of the universe sucked me in fast. The moral choices hit hard, and the game expects you to make tough calls with actual consequences.

If you loved WoTR, you’ll feel right at home. If you’re new to 40K? Honestly, this might be one of the best ways to get hooked. Owlcat really cooked with this one, flaws and all.

TL;DR: Zero 40K knowledge? Doesn’t matter. Owlcat carried hard. Highly recommend.

Also, because of this, I wishlisted Dark Heresy as soon as it's on the Steam Store!

Inform the dregs on the lower decks that the Lord Captain is most pleased. 

The only experience I had with warhammer prior to this game was reading the Eisenhorn trilogy and playing Space Marine 2, so I'm still a relative neophyte when it comes to singing the Emperor's praises. Owlcat in particular have a knack for constantly throwing unbelievably daunting challenges toward the player. I can think of no other developer who've made my player characters fight godlike creatures on so many occasions. 

You don't need to be a crpg enthusiast to enjoy this game. The writing is absolutely phenomenal, being both hilarious and deeply profound in many areas. name: Warhammer 40,000: Rogue Trader
review:
Less than 10 hours in at this point, but right now the game looks promising.

Trying to curb my min-max tendencies when leveling because I've no idea how these skills and stats are going to play out later in the game...but I'm starting to get a feel for it. And I'm not looking anything up online.

The world this is set in is absolutely fascinating. I don't have many hours in other WH40K games, but I think Owlcat did a great job capturing what the world is supposed to be about in terms of the overall design and, just, well the feel of the game. 

I just finished another run through of Xcom2 and this is a nice one to follow that up with. RT is a bit more cartoonish, for lack of a better term, and, to be frank, some of the dialog and scenarios that have popped up feel a bit cliched, but all this is also helping me to not worry about building the "perfect" character. The combat mechanics, and combat in general, have taken some getting used to. Or maybe it's just the play style I developed in the previous game that isn't working so well in this one. Owlcat has managed to make the combat in RT feel way more like a table top RPG than I was expecting. It seems like buffs and debuffs might be key in this game, making supps the OP characters, but right now, idk.

As a final thought: the game is good fun if you like tactical turn based games, table top miniature battles, or seeing this bizarre WH40K world. I'm going to log some more hours.

review:
What dice did right in this game, they did fantastically! The game feel, team orientation, classes, weapon choices, gun feel and quality sound of effects and the maps are just an absolute blast. Marvelous

What they did wrong they fucked up catastrophically! Spawning, some balancing issues and some weapon modifications are so useless or garbage it quickly overshadows what is great but most of all, the thing they did worst. 3D sound is less than terrible in this game. You will have literally tanks driving up next to you and not know before you are dead, every footstep is muffled beyond reason and snipers from 300 meters will sometimes be louder than literal airplanes and cars.



What is it like playing a game of battlefield V? Great! It honestly feels great, regardless of recon, medic or other classes, once you settle into how you like to play you realize you can cooperate and coordinate with your team to take points it plays very well and can be lots of fun with friends!... Then you realize people are spawning in between you and your allies for some reason, you hide only to get shot from 200 meters away by a tank who could not possibly have seen you, you go recon and someone halfway across the map will look away from the battlefield and the point and see you crawling through 1 meter tall grass and shot you. Hackers are so rampant that I genuinely cannot comprehend how devs can stand behind this type of blatant misuse. The worst part is that there is no appereant system implented, and reporting another player for cheating is a chore.

Overall, the game is 50% fun 50% going "yeah, sure yeah whatever, ok fine, I guess you can see me through 3 buildings"

review:
Steam forces me to pick a yes or no, I am mixed. Since the introduction of EA's anti-cheat, Javelin, things have changed.

Prior to Javelin, the game was unplayable. I genuinely mean that. Almost every lobby had a hacker, and they could click a button to send the entire lobby back to redeploy. It ruined countless games.

Since Javelin was rolled out, there are almost no hackers. I have only encountered one in the last 20 rounds I've played. It made it possible to play this game again.

However, there is a problem. I prefer to use Linux. With Javelin being kernel level anti-cheat this game is now impossible to play via Proton. This is where I wish EA had decided to use something like Easy Anti-Cheat, BattlEye, or even GameGuard. I am not a huge fan of kernel level anti-cheat but at least if they used a pre-existing one and didn't homebrew it themselves, it could still run on Linux.

It is unlikely that EA will ever make their anti-cheat compatible with Proton. I do dual-boot Windows, so the game is still accessible to me, but I immediately noticed how much worse the performance is on Windows. While I am glad to see the massive reduction of hackers, this still leaves a sour taste in my mouth.

review:
h1]🛸 R.E.P.O. - Realistically Evicting Poor Occupants[/h1]
[i]"I came for the aliens, I stayed for the soul-crushing capitalism."[/i]

So there I was, a fresh-faced space repo agent with nothing but a stun baton, a clipboard, and an absolutely shredded moral compass. My job? Repossess space junk from alien deadbeats who apparently never read the terms and conditions.

First mission: Evict a 7-foot grandma from her bio-dome because she missed two payments. She offered me cookies. I cooked her with a cart laser.

[b]10/10 realism.[/b] Feels just like working in corporate IT.

The game rewards efficiency and moral bankruptcy, so basically it’s a simulator for late-stage capitalism with aliens, monsters and your mentally challenged friends.

[i]If you’ve ever wanted to LARP as a sci-fi collections agent with questionable ethics and excellent fashion sense, this is your game. Just don’t ask where the tenants go after you beam them up. Probably to some other player’s unpaid storage locker.[/i]

[h3]Pros:[/h3]
– You get to yell "REPO!" and kick in spaceship doors.
– The paperwork is optional but the guilt is permanent.
– Surprisingly deep customization for a job that involves a lot of screaming.

[h3]Cons:[/h3]
– Emotionally I'm bankrupt.
– Accidentally beamed a child with 12 gauge shotgun. Got a promotion.
– One mentalist kept quoting space Karl Marx at me. I pretended to listen while looting his fish tank.

[hr][/hr]
[i]Final verdict:[/i]
[b]R.E.P.O. is not just a game — it’s a slowly decaying moral spiral you can upgrade with a plasma gun.[/b]
Would repo again. 10/10.

name: R.E.P.O.
review:
Overall, I feel like the Dev's made this game to troll the community. Anyway... Some spoilers in this review: 

It's a good game with friends. It has some bugs, issues with disconnection, even on a Lan, unfortunately. But overall it's fun. If you have a group of friends and just want to hang out for the evening then it's worth the $10, IMO. I haven't played with randoms yet, so I won't comment on that part.

But that's also the caveat, I marked it as I don't recommend yet because I mainly play it single player, and it's just a nightmare. Out of 200+ hours, they all ended in frustration. Not because it's hard from a skill perspective. That part is reasonable. Rather, it's got game mechanic issues, so you end up losing out of bad game happenstance more than monsters killing you, or even you falling into holes (happens so often, they could have just called it H.O.L.E.S. Hazardous Openings Loop Endless Suffering). Like, when you die in multiplayer, it's a laugh, when you die in single player and it's not your fault, it's like taming a creature in ARK for 8 hours, just to lose it right when it tames. Is that fun? Hard to say. But in ARK, you still have a base to go back to and cry, if you wanted. Overall, I'm going to give some props to the Devs. They chose a good art path, it has fair physics, definitely a neat idea and has fair to descent implementation. But my personally-experienced-beta-specific-issues are as follows:

Huntsman- needs to have a shorter gun or have his projectile launch point moved back a tad. (He can shoot through walls at the right angle, not corners either. Full walls.)

Gnomes- are not OP as an enemy, but they are OP from the stand point that they can ruin your run very quickly (Not a fun way to lose the match). Especially when they have an instant spawn timer, there are 8-12 of them and you now have exploding orbs in play. (I mean I get it, it's a loot game, and you "don't wanna let your loot get broken". Cool. But creatures that give nothing, shouldn't be that annoying.)

Peeper- just pisses me off. I feel like it's a solid creature and game mechanic, but I'd almost rather face any other enemy in the game.

Upscream - Good job Dev's for allowing us to jump at the end of his throw, that was hyper annoying not having any way to recover from the ambush.

Since the update, the other creatures feel fairly solid. Hidden seems to be less drunken, if that makes sense. Animal is definitely more annoying, but I accept it. Trudge seems excessive from an HP standpoint at higher game levels, as I charged all my Stam from 0 watching him bounce up and down inside a hole, over and over. With that high of HP, maybe he should be the only one worth 10k - 15k, and his soul is a giant half cart orb. At least that'd be funny.

Also... It's not cool when creatures spawn right next to you, or in the slight corner of the room you just came from 2 feet away, just because that "corner" is now, out of line of sight and maybe considered "The Next Room". I don't like fully programmed opposition in a game. Especially not in a game where you're not allowed to make one wrong move.

Lastly, I don't care for the resting physics either. These would be how items, or objects settle when you leave a room, then return. I get why it's needed for performance. But mixing bad resting physics, with exploding orbs, with dire don't make a single mistake consequences, isn't a good recipe for flavor. 

Final thoughts... Don't expect a hard core single player meta. But it's fun and worth it if you got co-op friends and just want to mess around. Keep in mind, I say all of this, with it being in Early access and in Beta, so we'll see the end result. I'll hop back around one day to check out the updates and perhaps change my review.

name: R.E.P.O.
review:
If you’re looking for another “Lethal-like” clone, keep scrolling R.E.P.O. is something else entirely. 

The physics system is both a blessing and a curse: stuff flies around, bodies ragdoll, and half the time you’re laughing at your own incompetence. It’s chaotic, it’s frustrating, and it’s exactly what makes this game a blast. The progression system is actually decent but i whish there where a bit more upgrades.

The graphics are clean, the atmosphere is on point, and the random chaos with friends or strangers just never gets old. 

And one thing that really sets R.E.P.O. apart is the audio. The spatial voice system is absolutely next level... when someone moves away, their voice gets muffled or distant, talk in a big room, and you instantly hear the echo and reverb. It sounds like a small detail, but it completely changes the vibe and keeps things fresh and hilarious every time.

Also, when someone talks, the character eyes lock onto whoever’s speaking. It’s such a small touch, but it adds a ton of personality and makes the whole experience feel way more alive.

Things I don’t like:

- Upgrades should apply to the whole team, not just the player who consume them.
- The balance between level difficulty and upgrades isn’t right progress gets way too hard, too fast.
- If you mess up collecting or turning in money, you can get stuck and have to start over, which kills the momentum.
- The game gets repetitive after a while, maybe unlocking special abilities or faster money at certain levels would help mix things up.
- There’s one map with a bunch of shafts you can easily fall into, it’s just frustrating and kind of ruins the fun.

BUT overall:
this game is pure, unfiltered fun. Highly recommended for anyone!

name: DayZ
review:
*This review is mostly based on DZSA modded servers since Vanilla DayZ is pure dehydration, starvation, disease, and death*

No other game scratches the *hardcore-survival-looter-shooter-prox-chat itch* like this game. The contrast of ultra realistic firearms ballistics, but with the jankiest world collision hitboxes & zombies, will either make you love or hate the game... for the DayZ veterans maybe a bit of both. It feels like a glitchy retro game but also modern sim at the same time.

Takes a while to get up and started with a base, pvp encounters are few and far between until you venture into cities/towns, but when you do encounter someone its pure adrenaline. One moment you're just running through the forest or looting a building, and the next thing you know you're in a gunfight holding 12 hours of loot and everything to lose, all while zombies are rushing towards you from a 100m away. No other game has made me more paranoid about losing my loot than DayZ although it gets better when you've established a base with storage. 

The sound of distant 1km away gunfire will give you a rush. The players are either the solo ghillie sniper, or the team who just rushes and flanks you on contact. If you're new, a lot of the times you won't know how you died (to that sniper) since it just cuts to black screen with no sound (can't hear the gunshot that killed you). Be prepared to use real world tactics & mechanics in this game to come out on top, eg. fire and maneuver, flanking, ambushing, concealment & cover, travelling in a spread out column formation with your group. Never sit still in the open in town. Even firearms mechanics like ballistics, zeroing, height over bore, etc. That or just rush in close range to spray and pray with an auto rifle. But seriously you'll save 100's of hours of pain, If you don't get the mechanics down in this game you're at a huge disadvantage.

p.s. Play modded servers on DZSA launcher and bring a friend.

review:
The first shots rang out somewhere to the south — sharp, distant, but close enough to draw me in.

I crept up the hill slow, rifle ready, stomach growling from starvation. I had barely anything left — my canteen was empty, my stomach hollow, and in my hand, a sniper rifle with one single bullet.

When I reached the top, I went prone and scanned the valley below.

A town — broken, quiet, crawling with infected. And there he was.

A survivor.

He moved cautiously through the town, checking each house. His gear looked solid. Backpack. Vest. Rifle slung over his shoulder. He was looting, calm but quick. I stayed flat in the hill, watching him through my scope for what felt like forever.

Seven minutes.

I followed his every move. House to house. No panic. No return fire. Just methodical scavenging. He had no idea he was being stalked.

Then he stopped — stepped behind a tree on the edge of town. Probably sorting his inventory. Vulnerable.

I adjusted my aim.

One bullet. One chance.

I took a breath, held it, and squeezed the trigger.

Crack.

He dropped instantly — like a puppet with its strings cut.

No hesitation. I leapt up and sprinted down the hill.

The infected would’ve heard that shot. Other players too. I didn’t have time to check.

I reached the body, snatched what I could — food, water, ammo, meds — then vanished back into the treeline before the echoes even died out.

That day, it all came down to patience and precision.

In DayZ, survival isn’t always about having more.

Sometimes, one bullet is enough.

review:
I have over 2k hours in this game just on this account on Steam, I've played this since 2013 on friends' PCs before I owned a PC. I played over 6k hours of DayZ on Playstation when that came out. I have purchased copies of this game for friends 5+ times over across different platforms. I think I'd probably recommend this to anyone who enjoys these 3 principle things in survival games: 
1. A hardcore survival or a completely customizable difficulty to your survival preference (with community modded servers). This game will push you to engage and learn on a curve that is very steep and sometimes makes you more thoughtful on your choices than you normally are on any other survival game. 
2. You have no UI (on a vanilla/lightly modded server) telling you to "get food" "get drink". Your story or character's "life" is up to you. You choose on what you want to accomplish and get no direction besides your character needs. 
3. You will die. A. LOT. and will be killed in the most ridiculous, stressful, and hilarious ways. But it makes you work to understand the game knowledge and how to survive longer. 

I love this game beyond measure, it's given me thousands of hours of entertainment and challenges. My favorite thing about this game, is that every character "life" is never the same. You can team up with people and become the biggest group on the server, you can team with other fresh spawns share food and water and get betrayed later on. You can become the bandit that you were killed by, You can steal peoples' shoes and amass a collection. You can do whatever you feel up to that minute and it'll feel different every time. I cannot speak higher of this games praises, legacy, and the love this community has. And hope everyone finds this review helpful and enjoys it half as much as I have. <3

review:
Fun until you get shot. Then it's fun again, until you get shot. Repeat until nothing is fun. Pretty much any good game could gain the same entertainment value of sudden inevitable death by setting a macro to randomly Alt+F4 for you and delete your save file. This one is not really optimized for Rogue-lite progress either; it's pretty much just Rogue-like FPS. That's common enough in PvP FPS, but you start with (basically) nothing every time, which leads into the enjoyable-enough survival crafting angle, but then randomly trashes all time invested, and it's generally enough time going into each life that it hurts. However, when you do manage to survive, or just play a community server without PvP or whatever, then it also becomes evident that the survival crafting angle doesn't actually go THAT deep anyway. Live or die, you're gonna be doing a lot of the same shit for as long as you have the appetite.

There are reasons to do it anyway, but those reasons are also too finite to justify all the mundane gripes of how actually unrealistic it is. E.g.: starving to death -- faster than you'd dehydrate -- in something like 2 hours of real time or maybe 2 days of game time -- and much faster if you're freezing, because...? Can't build a base or even drop a tent you're carrying because the ground isn't flat enough anywhere in sight? Chop down a tree of any size with a hatchet in 10 seconds, but you'll break all your hatchets, axes, sledgehammers, and maybe even your guns before you'll dent the wooden wall some jerk made out of the same kind of tree just to block off the water supply in the spawn towns, because fuck you.

And a big Fuck You Too to the playerbase. In 1212 hours, I've never had a 2-minute conversation with any of you psychos. The few of you willing to talk instead of shooting first are clearly too afraid that I'm going to kill you, and that's justified (mostly by others' baseline behavior). This game could've had all kinds of better social dynamics if you douchebags weren't wasting your lives preying on fresh spawns for some of the most pathetically invalid ego tripping PvP shooters have to offer, and that's saying something. May you all continue playing for tens and hundreds of thousands of hours until you're too physically infirm and cognitively rigid to do your harm anywhere else. DayZ can keep you.

name: Satisfactory
review:
Satisfactory is one of those games I really wanted to enjoy, and in some ways, I did—but it ended up being more frustrating than fun. I usually love games that let me control and fine-tune production systems, but this one just didn’t hit right, no matter how much I tried to get into it.

It definitely makes you think and plan ahead, which is great, but after a while it feels less like a game and more like a job. The early game is super slow, with hours spent gathering leaves and logs just to power your factory. Automated power takes way too long to unlock, and a lot of important upgrades are tied to random exploration, like finding colored rocks scattered across the map.

The blueprint system, which should make building easier, is really limited. Blueprints only fit one or two machines, they don’t link belts or power lines between sections, and you need a whole separate structure just to make them. That kind of defeats the purpose. And placing buildings manually every time gets tiring fast.

Resources are also super far apart, and the terrain makes it tough to build efficiently. Even something like steel production took me five hours to set up—and that was just one part of one tier. Most of that time was spent trial-and-erroring machine layouts, not actually progressing.

I think the game would be way better with friends, but only if everyone’s on the same page. Otherwise, clashing ideas would probably make things worse.

Overall, Satisfactory isn’t a bad game, but it’s definitely not for everyone. If you’re okay with a lot of grind and you don’t mind imperfect setups, you might enjoy it. But if you’re a perfectionist like me, it’ll probably just leave you feeling burned out and a little disappointed.

Amazing game. Best in genre AFAIK. The sheer scale of what you end up creating is spectacular. If you are skittish about complexity, I'd say there's at least 100h worth of gameplay before you burn out. If you enjoy that kind of stuff, man are you in for a treat. I'm 250h in, the end is in sight, but what a ride.  It's pretty polished, with minor bugs and annoyances showing up very late in the game. The usability and UX is pretty impressive for something this complex and rich system wise. 

I waited a loooong time for controller support before playing this and boy was I not disappointed. Seriously other devs should take notes. This isn't perfect but it's a masterclass in how to adapt a complex and control heavy M+KB game to controller. I'm still laughing about people saying "just use steam inputs to remap, it doesn't need controller support".  LOL, I hope they play 1.1 and understand what controller support means.

If you are the least interested based on the genre, premise and screenshots, just play it.  Plus the humor works and the AI assistant is fun in a portal kinda way.

It's gets a bit mathy at the end there. I would say that nuclear power (which you can skip if you do turbo fuel at scale) was a bit beyond enjoyable in terms of complexity, but man, is it a beauty to watch it run afterward. Aluminum with the water feedback loop is also temperamental and annoying. I also skipped trains, which I didn't felt I really needed (given quick personal runs with a full inventory on ziplines) and once I needed it, I had discovered drones, so I did that instead. But it's a whole other system to explore and play with.

So in the end... just... wow. Probably the best game I'll have played this year, barring a huge surprise.

NBA 2K20 continues the franchise’s tradition of delivering a highly realistic basketball simulation, with stellar visuals, tight gameplay, and robust content. However, it’s not without its flaws.

Graphics and Presentation: Stunning visuals and lifelike player animations capture the essence of the NBA, while dynamic commentary keeps the experience immersive.
MyCareer Mode: A compelling storyline with celebrity involvement adds depth, alongside satisfying customization options for your player.
Variety of Modes: From MyTeam to MyLeague, there’s plenty of content to keep players engaged, whether you prefer competitive online play or managing a franchise.

Cons:
Microtransactions: Heavy reliance on in-game purchases in modes like MyTeam and MyCareer detracts from the enjoyment, especially for casual players.
Repetitiveness: Despite small updates, gameplay can feel overly familiar for long-time fans.
Server Issues: Online connectivity remains inconsistent, which can be frustrating for multiplayer enthusiasts.

Verdict:
NBA 2K20 shines in gameplay and presentation but stumbles with aggressive monetization and recurring technical hiccups. It’s an excellent choice for basketball fans who can overlook its shortcomings. Rating: 7.5/10.

In conclusion, NBA 2K20 for PC has been marred by technical issues, rampant cheating, and inadequate developer response to these problems. While the game may offer some enjoyment in its offline modes, the online experience falls short of expectations due to the lack of effective anti-cheating measures and the resulting toxic environment.

Honestly, I can’t imagine even basketball legends like Shaquille O'Neal would call this game anything but trash - he’d probably take a sledgehammer to a copy, smash it to pieces, and then set it aflame! The company keeps releasing the same game year after year, milking fans dry while delivering nothing new. No one should buy this game! I’d rather burn money, set my house aflame, or destroy all my clothes than endure this mess again. I’d happily shatter every window in my home and watch it be torn down instead of playing this game for another minute.

Letting myself be bitten by a snake sounds more appealing than facing the clunky gameplay and endless glitches. I’d rather stub my toe repeatedly, fail all my exams, or have all my life’s hard work be destroyed than deal with this disaster. I’d even willingly get my leg amputated or spend a week in a jail cell rather than suffer through NBA 2K20. Honestly, I’d rather be eaten by lions than put up with this game!

I’d gladly take a sledgehammer to my TV, dig a hole in my backyard, or scrub my floors with a toothbrush just to escape this non-functional mess. Cleaning out a filthy garage, organizing my sock drawer, or listening to elevator music for hours sounds like a welcome distraction. The thought of watching paint dry or listening to a lecture on tax law feels like a treat compared to this. I’d rather clean my gutters, deal with a flat tire, or spend an entire weekend cleaning the attic than endure NBA 2K20.

It’s an insult to basketball fans everywhere, and it deserves to be buried and forgotten! Do yourself a favor and steer clear of this game - it’s nothing more than a cash grab wrapped in flashy graphics!

Despite repeated attempts to engage with this game, for some reason it lacks a lot of the charm of the original. Because of the nature of the balance between DPS and survivability, most of the time my deaths felt completely out of nowhere and were basically one hit KOs that dealt my full life bar in a single shot. 

For some reason navigating in 3D space feels more cumbersome than the 2D of the original, and the graphics are just straight up less interesting to look at, with tons of empty space filled with bland textures. The game also lacks usability functions in navigating the item compendium or assisting players in remembering what items actually do. And a lot of the extra path stuff feels very cryptic, as though it necessitates a guide.

Overall just not a game that resulted in much fun, whereas the original Risk of Rain is one of my favorite indie rogue-lites of all time.

name: EA SPORTS FIFA 23
review:
FIFA 23 marks the end of an era—the last game in the iconic franchise under the FIFA name before EA transitions to EA SPORTS FC. It’s a moment loaded with legacy and expectation, and while FIFA 23 doesn’t completely revolutionize the formula, it delivers a polished, feature-rich, and enjoyable football experience that feels like a well-timed volley into the top corner—if not quite a game-winner from midfield.

FIFA 23 builds on the refined gameplay of FIFA 22 with the introduction of HyperMotion2 technology (on next-gen platforms), offering more fluid animations, improved ball physics, and better player responsiveness. It’s a noticeable step up in realism—players feel weightier, passes zip with more purpose, and off-the-ball movement is much smarter.

The pace is slower and more tactical than older FIFA titles, rewarding build-up play and intelligent positioning over pure sprint-speed abuse. Defending is more manual and demanding, while finishing has been balanced with new power shots—high-risk, high-reward strikes that look and feel fantastic when pulled off.

Still, the classic FIFA quirks are present. Occasionally chaotic physics, questionable AI choices, and some overpowered meta tactics (hello, trivela shots) remind you this is still, ultimately, FIFA.

Career Mode sees welcome, if modest, improvements. The addition of Playable Highlights lets you jump into key moments instead of full matches—great for those who want to speed through seasons. You can now play as real-world managers like Pep Guardiola or Jürgen Klopp, adding some cosmetic flair, though it doesn’t affect gameplay.

Player Career gets a light RPG touch with personality traits that influence your growth and endorsement deals, but it still lacks real narrative depth. Overall, Career Mode remains enjoyable and feature-rich—but feels overdue for a bigger overhaul.

FUT remains a polished and dangerously addictive experience. New to FIFA 23 is the revamped Chemistry System, which gives more flexibility when building squads, no longer restricting players to strict positional links. This change opens up more creativity and eases the squad-building experience.

FUT Moments is a fun new single-player mode offering quick, objective-based challenges with bite-sized gameplay. It’s great for casual players and makes earning rewards a bit more engaging.

Of course, FUT still leans heavily on microtransactions, and pay-to-win concerns linger. If you don’t invest real money, you’ll be grinding for top-tier squads longer than you'd like.

One of FIFA 23’s most genuinely progressive additions is the expanded focus on women’s football. For the first time, you can play with fully licensed women’s club teams from the Barclays Women’s Super League and D1 Arkema, and they’re more than a reskin—animations, tactics, and feel are unique.

EA also included both the FIFA Men’s and Women’s World Cups as playable modes, giving the game more international flavor and variety.

As always, FIFA nails the atmosphere. From the broadcast-style overlays and authentic crowd chants to stadium lighting and commentary, this is peak sports presentation. The visuals are slick—especially on next-gen—with detailed kits, player likenesses, and realistic pitch wear.

The soundtrack is also excellent, featuring a diverse, global mix that feels fitting for the final game in the FIFA era.

Where It Impresses
-Slower, more realistic gameplay with HyperMotion2
-Expanded women’s football and World Cup modes
-Playable Highlights and improved Career pacing
-Better chemistry system in FUT
-Incredible presentation, as expected

Where It Falls Short
-Career Mode still lacks true innovation
-FUT remains grind-heavy and monetized
-Occasional gameplay quirks and meta exploits
-Legacy issues in AI and refereeing persist

FIFA 23 is a strong and satisfying sendoff for the franchise that shaped football gaming for nearly three decades. It doesn’t reinvent the sport, but it polishes nearly every part of the experience, delivering the most feature-complete FIFA to date. It’s a celebration of the sport, the brand, and the players—digital and real.

Whether you’re a FUT addict, a Career Mode lifer, or just someone who loves kicking off a match with friends, FIFA 23 has enough to keep your boots on the virtual pitch.

A respectful farewell to a footballing legacy.

Rating: 7/10
